experiments.title: Find Your Blind Spot
experiments.hook: Every one of us has a hole in our vision right now, and our brain paints over it so we never notice.

grown.try: Close your RIGHT eye. Stare at the + with your left eye only. Slowly move your face toward the screen (or away). At one distance the red dot will vanish completely.
grown.why: At the back of each eye, the optic nerve and the retina's blood supply pass through one spot that has no light-detecting cells (no rods or cones). Any image that lands there simply isn't detected. Your brain fills the gap with whatever surrounds it, which is why Level 2's line looks unbroken even when the dot is gone.

kids.try: Cover your RIGHT eye. Look ONLY at the + . Now slowly lean closer to the screen. Keep looking at the +! At just the right spot... the red dot disappears!
kids.why: Poof! Your eye has a tiny spot with no seeing cells, right where the cable to your brain (the optic nerve) plugs in. When the dot lands there, your eye can't see it. Your brain fills in the hole so sneakily that you never notice it in real life!

experiments.realworld: You never notice your blind spot in daily life because your brain fills it in, and with both eyes open, each eye sees what the other one misses.

steps: Draw a + on the left and a dot about 3 inches to the right.
Hold the card at arm's length and close your right eye.
Stare at the + and slowly bring the card closer until the dot vanishes.

sources.title: American Academy of Ophthalmology: Blind Spot
Exploratorium: Blind Spot (Science Snack)
Exploratorium: Seeing Your Blind Spot

experiments.title: The Two Squares That Are the Same
experiments.hook: Your eyes don't measure brightness. They compare it, and that comparison can fool you completely.

grown.try: Look at the two small squares. One looks clearly lighter than the other. Then tap the button to remove the background.
grown.why: Both squares are the exact same gray. This is called simultaneous contrast: how light a patch looks depends on what surrounds it. On a dark background the gray looks lighter; on a light background it looks darker. Your visual system is built to judge things relative to their surroundings, which usually helps you, but here it misleads you.

kids.try: Which little square is lighter? Decide! Now tap the button to take the background away.
kids.why: Surprise! They're the SAME gray! Your eyes compare each square to what's around it. Next to dark, gray looks lighter. Next to light, gray looks darker. Your brain got tricked!

experiments.realworld: Designers and painters deal with this constantly: the same paint color can look different depending on the wall or colors next to it.

needs: Gray paper (or a gray paint chip)
steps: Cut two small squares from the same gray paper.
Put one on the black sheet and one on the white sheet.
Compare them side by side. Then hold them together off the backgrounds.
home.safety: Kids: ask a grown-up to help with scissors.

sources.title: University of Minnesota: Simultaneous Contrast (Sensation and Perception)
University of British Columbia: Simultaneous Contrast: Luminance
MIT Brain and Cognitive Sciences: Study sheds light on a classic visual illusion

experiments.title: How Fast Are You, Really?
experiments.hook: Even a fast reaction takes about a fifth of a second. At highway speed, that's a car length before your foot even moves.

grown.try: Tap Start. When the box turns GREEN, tap it as fast as you can. Do 5 rounds and see your average.
grown.why: Your eyes detect the change, the signal travels to your brain, your brain decides, and a signal travels back down to your finger. A careful 2015 study of 1,469 adults measured an average simple reaction time of 231 milliseconds (213 ms after correcting for computer delay), and it slowly increases with age. Phones and screens add their own delay, so web tests usually read a bit slower than lab tests.

kids.try: Tap Start. Wait... wait... when the box turns GREEN, tap it super fast! Try 5 times!
kids.why: Zoom! Your eyes see green, send a message to your brain, your brain says GO, and a message zips to your finger. All that takes about a quarter of a second for most grown-ups. Blink and you'd miss it!

experiments.realworld: At 60 mph a car travels about 88 feet every second, so a quarter-second reaction means roughly 22 feet before a driver even touches the brake.

steps: Your partner holds the ruler at the top; you hold your thumb and finger open around the bottom (at 0).
Without warning, your partner drops it. Catch it as fast as you can.
The inch mark where you caught it shows your reaction. Shorter drop = faster!

sources.title: Frontiers in Human Neuroscience (Woods et al., 2015): Factors influencing the latency of simple reaction time
Encyclopedia.com: Reaction Time

experiments.title: Your Brain Can't Stop Reading
experiments.hook: Reading is so automatic that your brain does it even when you're trying NOT to, and it costs you time.

grown.try: Tap the button that matches the INK COLOR of each word, not the word itself. Round 1 is easy. Round 2 is where it gets interesting. Compare your times.
grown.why: This is the Stroop effect, published by psychologist John Ridley Stroop in 1935. Reading is automatic and overlearned, while naming a color takes deliberate attention. When the word and ink clash, your brain has to suppress the urge to read, and that conflict slows you down and causes more mistakes. It's one of the most studied effects in psychology and is still used in research and clinical testing.

kids.try: Tap the button for the COLOR of the letters, not what the word says! Round 1, then Round 2. Which one was harder?
kids.why: Gotcha! Your brain reads words automatically, super fast, even when you tell it not to. When the word says RED but the letters are blue, your brain argues with itself, and that slows you down!

experiments.realworld: Scientists still use this test today to study attention and how the brain handles distractions.

steps: Write 10 color words in the SAME color as the word (RED in red).
Write 10 more where the ink doesn't match (RED in blue).
Time yourself saying the ink colors out loud for each list.

sources.title: Science Buddies: Seeing Science: Exploring Perception with the Stroop Effect
PsyToolkit: The Stroop task
Wikipedia: Stroop effect

experiments.title: The Flag That Changes Color
experiments.hook: Stare at a strange-colored flag, look away, and your own eyes will paint the real one in red, white and blue.

grown.try: Stare at the small dot in the middle of the flag without moving your eyes until the countdown ends. The flag will disappear. Keep staring at the dot.
grown.why: Your retina has cone cells tuned to red, green and blue light. Staring at one color fatigues the cones that detect it, so they respond less for a few seconds. When you then look at white, the rested cones dominate and you see the opposite (complementary) colors. Cyan becomes red, black becomes white, and yellow becomes blue.

kids.try: Stare at the little dot in the middle. Don't move your eyes! When the timer ends, keep staring...
kids.why: Whoa! The color-seeing cells in your eyes got tired from staring. When you look at white, the tired cells take a break and the other cells take over, so you see the OPPOSITE colors. Red, white and blue appear out of nowhere!

experiments.realworld: This is one reason surgeons wear blue-green scrubs: it reduces the distracting afterimages from staring at red blood.

needs: A red paper shape (like a bird or heart)
steps: Stare at the red shape for 30 seconds.
Quickly look at the plain white paper.
Watch for a blue-green copy of the shape!
home.safety: Never stare at the Sun or any bright light.

sources.title: Science Buddies: Afterimages and cone cell fatigue
Exploratorium: Bird in the Cage (Science Snack)
Science News Explores: Discover the science behind afterimages

experiments.title: Your Nose Does the Tasting
experiments.hook: Most of what you call 'taste' is actually smell. Hold your nose and a cherry jelly bean just tastes sweet.
experiments.predict: Hold your nose and eat a jelly bean. Will you still know the flavor?
experiments.reveal: Most people can tell it's sweet (and maybe sour), but can't name the flavor. The moment they let go of their nose, the flavor suddenly floods in.

grown.try: Grab two jelly beans of different flavors. Pinch your nose shut, chew one, and try to name the flavor. Then let go and keep chewing.
grown.why: Your tongue only detects basic tastes like sweet, sour, salty, bitter and savory. The specific flavor (strawberry, cinnamon, cherry) comes from odor molecules that travel from your mouth up the back of your nose to your smell cells. Pinch your nose and that airflow stops, so all that's left is the basic taste.

kids.try: Pinch your nose. Chew a jelly bean. What flavor is it? Now let go of your nose!
kids.why: Sniff-tastic! Your tongue can only tell sweet, sour, salty and bitter. The real flavor, like cherry or lemon, comes from smells floating up to your nose from the back of your mouth. No smell = no flavor!

experiments.realworld: This is why food tastes bland when you have a stuffy nose from a cold.

needs: Jelly beans in different flavors (or apple and pear slices)
A partner (optional, for a blindfold test)
steps: Pinch your nose closed and chew one jelly bean for a few seconds.
Guess the flavor.
Let go of your nose and keep chewing. Did the flavor change?
home.safety: Check for food allergies first.

sources.title: Scientific American: How do sight and smell affect taste?
Scientific American / Science Buddies: Jelly Bean Taste Test
The Franklin Institute: Jelly Bean Taste Test

experiments.title: The Hammer and the Feather
experiments.hook: In 1971 an astronaut dropped a hammer and a feather on the Moon. They hit the ground at exactly the same time.

grown.try: Drop the hammer and feather on Earth, then on the Moon. Watch which lands first in each place.
grown.why: Gravity pulls on every object with the same acceleration, no matter its mass. On Earth, air pushes back on the light, wide feather far more than on the hammer, so the feather drifts. The Moon has almost no atmosphere, so nothing slows the feather. On Aug. 2, 1971, Apollo 15 commander David Scott dropped a 1.32 kg geologic hammer and a falcon feather from about 1.6 m, and they landed together, just as Galileo predicted.

kids.try: Drop them on Earth first. Then try the Moon!
kids.why: Whoa! On the Moon there's no air to slow the feather down, so it falls just as fast as the heavy hammer. Gravity pulls on everything the same way. It's the air that makes feathers float on Earth!

experiments.realworld: Engineers test parachutes and spacecraft in huge vacuum chambers to remove air resistance, just like the Moon did for Scott.

needs: A small square of paper (smaller than the coin)
steps: Drop the coin and the paper side by side. The coin wins.
Now lay the paper flat on top of the coin.
Drop them together. The coin blocks the air, and the paper falls just as fast.

sources.title: NASA NSSDCA: The Apollo 15 Hammer-Feather Drop
NASA Science: The Apollo 15 Hammer-Feather Drop
NASA Planetary Fact Sheet (Moon gravity 1.6 m/s²)

experiments.title: The Paper That Falls Like a Book
experiments.hook: A flat sheet of paper floats down slowly, but put it on top of a book and it drops just as fast as the book.

grown.try: Drop a book and a sheet of paper side by side. Then lay the paper on top of the book and drop them together.
grown.why: Gravity accelerates the book and the paper the same way. The difference is air resistance: a flat sheet has a lot of surface for its tiny mass, so the air slows it a lot. When the paper rides on top of the book, the book pushes the air out of the way and the paper never feels the drag, so both fall at the book's rate.

kids.try: Drop a book and a paper at the same time. Then put the paper ON the book and drop again!
kids.why: Ta-da! The book acts like a shield and pushes the air away. Without air in its way, the paper falls just as fast as the heavy book!

experiments.realworld: Skydivers use the same idea in reverse: spreading out catches more air and slows them down.

needs: A sheet of paper smaller than the book
steps: Drop the book and the flat paper side by side from the same height.
Place the paper flat on top of the book.
Drop them together and watch the paper.

sources.title: Simon Fraser University Physics: Book and Paper Drop
University of Colorado Physics Lab Demos: Book and Paper
TeachEngineering: How Do Things Fall?

experiments.predict: When the paper sits on top of the book, will it fall slower, the same, or faster?
experiments.reveal: The paper stays on the book and they land together. The book clears the air out of the paper's way.

experiments.title: The Coin That Refuses to Move
experiments.hook: Flick a card out from under a coin and the coin drops straight down into the cup, as if it never felt a thing.

grown.try: Put a playing card on top of a cup and a coin on the card. Flick the card sideways, quickly and firmly.
grown.why: This is Newton's first law, also called inertia: an object at rest stays at rest unless a force acts on it. A fast flick gives friction almost no time to drag the coin along, so the coin stays put while the card shoots away. Then gravity pulls the coin straight down into the cup. It's the same physics as the famous tablecloth trick.

kids.try: Coin on a card, card on a cup. FLICK the card fast!
kids.why: Plop! The coin is lazy (scientists call it inertia). It wants to stay right where it is, so when the card zooms away, the coin just drops into the cup!

experiments.realworld: Inertia is why you lurch forward when a car stops suddenly, and why seat belts matter.

needs: A playing card or index card
steps: Lay the card flat across the cup and center the coin on it.
Hold the cup steady with one hand.
Flick the edge of the card sharply and straight sideways.

sources.title: University of Maryland Physics Lecture Demos: Tablecloth (coin and card)
Carleton College SERC: Newton's First Law (Inertia)

experiments.predict: When you flick the card away, will the coin fly with it or drop into the cup?
experiments.reveal: With a quick, level flick, the coin drops right into the cup. A slow pull drags the coin along instead.

experiments.title: The Egg That Spins Itself Again
experiments.hook: Stop a spinning raw egg with your finger, let go, and it starts spinning again all by itself.

grown.try: Spin a hard-boiled egg and a raw egg. Then stop each one with a fingertip for a second and let go.
grown.why: Inside a hard-boiled egg everything is solid, so it spins smoothly and stops all at once. A raw egg is liquid inside. When you stop the shell, the liquid keeps swirling because of inertia, and when you let go it drags the shell back into motion. NASA's JPL uses this same activity to teach Newton's first law.

kids.try: Spin both eggs. Tap to stop them. Let go fast. Which one starts again?
kids.why: Spooky! The raw egg's gooey inside keeps swirling even when the shell stops, so it gets the shell spinning again. The cooked egg is solid and just stays stopped!

experiments.realworld: It's a real kitchen trick: you can tell a hard-boiled egg from a raw one without cracking it.

steps: Spin each egg on its side and watch: the cooked one spins fast and smooth.
While each spins, touch the top briefly to stop it.
Lift your finger right away and watch for a second spin.
home.safety: Kids: ask a grown-up to boil the egg.

sources.title: NASA JPL Education: Planetary Egg Wobble and Newton's First Law
Science World: Egg Spinning
Indiana Public Media A Moment of Science: The Spin Test

experiments.predict: After you stop them, which egg will start moving again?
experiments.reveal: The raw egg starts turning again on its own. The hard-boiled egg stays stopped.

experiments.title: The Water That Won't Fall Out
experiments.hook: The air around you is pushing on everything with enough force to hold a glass of water upside down.

grown.try: Over a sink, fill a glass with water, cover it with an index card, flip it, and let go of the card.
grown.why: Air pressure pushes on the card from below. As soon as a tiny bit of water starts to leak, the air trapped inside spreads into more space and its pressure drops, so the outside air pushes harder than the water pushes down. Surface tension also helps seal the wet card to the rim. Together they hold the water in.

kids.try: Do this over the sink! Glass of water, card on top, flip, and let go of the card.
kids.why: Magic? Nope, air! The air in the room is pushing up on the card super hard, harder than the water is pushing down. So the water stays put!

experiments.realworld: Air pressure is also what lets a drinking straw work: you lower the pressure inside and the air outside pushes the drink up.

needs: An index card or playing card
steps: Fill the cup with water, right to the top for the best results.
Press the card firmly onto the rim.
Hold the card, flip the cup over the sink, then slowly let go of the card.
home.safety: Practice over a sink. Plastic cups are safest.

sources.title: Science in School: Experimenting with water (upside-down glass)
Museum of Science, Boston: Water Defies Gravity
Royal Society of Chemistry: Air pressure activity

experiments.predict: When you let go of the card, will the water pour out?
experiments.reveal: The card stays and the water stays in, until air sneaks in at the edge. Then: splash!

experiments.title: Your Fingers Always Find the Middle
experiments.hook: Slide your fingers together under a yardstick and they always meet at its balance point, no matter where they start.

grown.try: Rest a yardstick on your two index fingers, far apart and uneven. Slowly slide your fingers toward each other.
grown.why: The finger closer to the center carries more of the stick's weight, so it has more friction and grips. The farther finger carries less weight and slides. As it slides closer, it takes on more weight and grips, and the other finger slides instead. They take turns until they meet under the center of gravity, every time.

kids.try: Put a yardstick on two fingers. Slide your fingers together slowly. Where do they meet?
kids.why: Every time, right in the middle! Your fingers take turns sliding and sticking, and they always end up at the balance point. Try to stop it. You can't!

experiments.realworld: Engineers locate the center of gravity of cars, planes and cranes to keep them stable and balanced.

needs: A yardstick, meter stick or broom handle
steps: Hold your index fingers out, wide apart, with the stick resting on them.
Start with one finger much closer to an end than the other.
Slowly slide your fingers together and watch which one moves.

sources.title: Exploratorium: Center of Gravity (Science Snack)
Simon Fraser University Physics: Metre Stick on Fingers

experiments.predict: If one finger starts near the end, where will your fingers meet?
experiments.reveal: They meet at the center of gravity every time. The fingers take turns sliding.

experiments.title: The Cabbage Rainbow
experiments.hook: Red cabbage juice can turn into almost every color of the rainbow, depending on what you mix in.

grown.try: Slide from acid to base and watch the cabbage juice change color.
grown.why: Red cabbage contains pigments called anthocyanins that change shape, and color, depending on how acidic or basic a solution is. That makes cabbage juice a natural pH indicator. Science Buddies lists the colors as red near pH 2, purple at 4, violet at 6, blue at 8, blue-green at 10 and greenish-yellow at 12.

kids.try: Slide the bar and watch the colors change!
kids.why: Color magic! Cabbage juice has a secret color-changer inside. Sour stuff like vinegar turns it pink or red. Stuff like baking soda turns it blue or green!

experiments.realworld: The same kind of pigment helps make some flowers and fruits different colors.

steps: A grown-up soaks the chopped cabbage in hot water for 10 minutes, then strains out the purple juice.
Pour a little juice into several clear cups.
Add vinegar to one, baking soda to another, and lemon juice to a third. Compare the colors.
home.safety: Never mix cleaning products. Stick to kitchen items like vinegar, lemon and baking soda.

sources.title: Science Buddies: Cabbage pH Indicator
Royal Society of Chemistry: Red cabbage pH indicator experiments
TeachEngineering: Acid and Base Rainbows

experiments.title: The Balloon That Blows Itself Up
experiments.hook: You can inflate a balloon without blowing, just by mixing two things from your kitchen.

grown.try: Put baking soda in a balloon, stretch it over a bottle of vinegar, and tip the powder in.
grown.why: Vinegar (an acid) reacts with baking soda (a base). The reaction makes new substances, including carbon dioxide gas, which has nowhere to go but into the balloon. More baking soda and vinegar make more gas. Bonus: carbon dioxide is heavier than the air you breathe out, so a CO2 balloon falls faster than one you blow up.

kids.try: Baking soda in the balloon, vinegar in the bottle. Tip it in and watch!
kids.why: Fizz-tastic! When vinegar and baking soda meet, they make a brand-new gas called carbon dioxide. It fills up the balloon all by itself!

experiments.realworld: Baking soda makes cakes rise for the same reason: its gas bubbles puff up the batter.

steps: Pour about half a cup of vinegar into the bottle.
Use a funnel to put 2 spoonfuls of baking soda into the balloon.
Stretch the balloon over the bottle top, then lift it so the baking soda falls in.

sources.title: American Chemical Society: More Than Hot Air
Science Buddies: How Heavy Is Your Air?
Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum: Baking Soda Balloon Blast

experiments.predict: What will happen to the balloon when the baking soda falls into the vinegar?
experiments.reveal: The mixture fizzes and the balloon inflates as carbon dioxide gas fills it.

experiments.title: Toothpaste for an Elephant
experiments.hook: A tiny living thing, yeast, can make a fountain of foam shoot out of a bottle in seconds.

grown.try: Mix yeast with warm water, then pour it into a bottle of 3% hydrogen peroxide with a squirt of dish soap.
grown.why: Hydrogen peroxide slowly breaks down into water and oxygen on its own. Yeast contains an enzyme called catalase, a catalyst that speeds that breakdown up enormously. The burst of oxygen gets trapped in the dish soap, making a foam. The bottle also feels warm, because the reaction releases heat.

kids.try: Yeast + warm water, then pour it into the peroxide and soap. Stand back!
kids.why: Whoosh! Yeast has a helper inside called catalase that breaks the peroxide into water and oxygen super fast. The soap traps the oxygen in bubbles. Foam fountain!

experiments.realworld: Catalase is in almost all living things, including you. It's why peroxide bubbles on a scrape.

steps: Mix the yeast with a few spoonfuls of warm water and wait a minute.
Pour about half a cup of hydrogen peroxide into the bottle and add a squirt of dish soap.
Pour in the yeast mix and step back.
home.safety: Grown-up needed. Wear safety glasses; peroxide irritates eyes. Use only 3% store-bought peroxide. The foam is not toothpaste.

sources.title: Scientific American / Science Buddies: How to Make Elephant Toothpaste
USDA Agricultural Research Service: Elephant Toothpaste

experiments.predict: What do you think will come out of the bottle?
experiments.reveal: Thick foam pours out within seconds, and the bottle feels warm.

experiments.title: From Dull Penny to Shiny Penny
experiments.hook: The 'dirt' on an old penny isn't dirt at all. It's a brand-new chemical that formed on the metal.

grown.try: Soak dull pennies in vinegar mixed with a teaspoon of salt, then rinse half of them and leave half unrinsed.
grown.why: Copper reacts with oxygen in the air to form copper oxide, the dull brown layer. A weak acid plus table salt dissolves that oxide, revealing shiny copper. Pennies left unrinsed often turn blue-green later, as the exposed copper reacts again with air and chloride from the salt. The U.S. Mint notes that pennies made before 1982 contain more copper, so their reactions are more visible.

kids.try: Soak pennies in salty vinegar. Rinse some, don't rinse others. Check them later!
kids.why: Shine time! The brown on old pennies is copper oxide, made when copper meets air. Vinegar and salt wash it away. The unrinsed ones might even turn green later!

experiments.realworld: That green coat is why the Statue of Liberty is green: its copper skin reacted with the air over many years.

steps: Mix the salt into the vinegar in the bowl.
Drop in the pennies and wait about a minute.
Rinse half and dry them; put the other half on a towel unrinsed. Check again in an hour.

sources.title: Science Buddies: Shine Bright Like a Penny
American Chemical Society: Let's Do Chemistry with the Penny
U.S. Mint: Clean or Green Pennies

experiments.predict: What will happen to the pennies you don't rinse?
experiments.reveal: The rinsed pennies stay shiny. The unrinsed ones often develop a blue-green coating.

experiments.title: The Exploding Milk Rainbow
experiments.hook: One touch of dish soap makes food coloring race across a plate of milk.

grown.try: Put drops of food coloring on a plate of milk, then touch the center with a cotton swab dipped in dish soap.
grown.why: Dish soap is mostly surfactants, which lower the surface tension of the milk. Where the soap touches, surface tension drops, and the higher surface tension all around pulls the milk, and the colors, away. The soap also breaks up fat in the milk, which keeps the colors swirling. Use milk with fat; non-fat milk works poorly.

kids.try: Colors on milk, soapy swab in the middle. Watch!
kids.why: Kaboom of color! The soap breaks the milk's stretchy 'skin' and grabs onto the fat, so the colors zoom away and swirl!

experiments.realworld: This is exactly how dish soap cleans greasy plates: it grabs fat and breaks it up.

steps: Pour a thin layer of milk onto the plate.
Add drops of different food coloring near the center.
Dip the swab in soap and touch it to the middle of the milk. Hold it there.

sources.title: Science Buddies: Milk Rainbow
Scientific American: Surfactant Science: Make a Milk Rainbow

experiments.predict: What will the colors do when the soap touches the milk?
experiments.reveal: The colors burst outward and swirl for a while as the soap spreads.

experiments.title: Grow Your Own Crystals
experiments.hook: Hot water can hold far more sugar than cold water. As it cools, that extra sugar builds giant crystals.

grown.try: With a grown-up, dissolve as much sugar as possible in boiling water, then let it cool around a sugar-coated stick for a week.
grown.why: Heating water lets it dissolve much more sugar. As the solution cools, it holds more sugar than it normally could, which is called supersaturated. That's unstable, so sugar molecules come out of the solution and stack onto the seed crystals on your stick, growing larger crystals over days.

kids.try: Super-sweet water plus a sugary stick plus time = crystals!
kids.why: Sweet science! Hot water can hold tons of sugar. When it cools down, the extra sugar has to go somewhere, so it builds crystals on your stick!

experiments.realworld: Candy makers control crystal growth on purpose: it's the difference between smooth fudge and grainy fudge.

steps: Wet the skewer, roll it in sugar, and let it dry: these are your seed crystals.
A grown-up heats the water and stirs in sugar until no more will dissolve, then lets it cool for 15 minutes and pours it into the jar.
Hang the skewer in the jar with the clothespin, not touching the bottom. Wait 5 to 7 days.
home.safety: Grown-up needed: boiling sugar syrup causes severe burns.

sources.title: Carolina Biological: Rock Candy, An Edible Study of Crystallization
Australian National University: How to make rock candy
Science News Explores: Rock Candy Science

experiments.predict: Will the crystals grow faster in the first day or later in the week?
experiments.reveal: Small crystals appear within a day or two and keep growing for about a week.

experiments.title: Make a Cloud in a Jar
experiments.hook: Every cloud needs three things: warm moist air, cooling, and specks of dust for water to cling to.

grown.try: With a grown-up, put warm water in a jar, cover it with ice, and add a puff of particles (like a quick spray of hairspray).
grown.why: Warm water evaporates and fills the jar with moist air. The ice cools the air at the top, so the water vapor wants to condense. It needs something to condense on, called condensation nuclei, which the particles supply. Billions of tiny droplets form: a real cloud. Lift the lid and it drifts out.

kids.try: Warm water, icy lid, a tiny spray. Watch a cloud appear!
kids.why: Poof, a cloud! Warm wet air rises, the ice cools it, and the water grabs onto tiny specks in the air. That's exactly how clouds are made in the sky!

experiments.realworld: Real clouds form on dust, sea salt and smoke particles high in the atmosphere.

needs: Hairspray or a match blown out (grown-up)
steps: Pour about 1/3 cup of warm water into the jar and swirl it.
Flip the lid upside down, fill it with ice, and set it on the jar.
Lift the lid briefly, add a quick spray of hairspray, and replace it. Watch the cloud form, then lift the lid to release it.
home.safety: Grown-up needed for hot water.

sources.title: NASA JPL Education: Make a Cloud in a Bottle
UCAR Center for Science Education: Cloud in a Jar
Ingenium Canada: Cloud in a Jar

experiments.predict: What will you see inside the jar after the spray?
experiments.reveal: A gray, swirling cloud forms and drifts out when the lid is lifted.

experiments.title: A Tornado in a Bottle
experiments.hook: A swirl of water can make a funnel that looks just like a tornado, and it drains faster than still water.

grown.try: Connect two bottles neck to neck, one with water, flip them, and swirl the top bottle in circles.
grown.why: Swirling sets the water spinning around a center, called a vortex. The spinning water moves outward, opening a channel in the middle where air can rise into the top bottle while water spirals down. That's why a swirled bottle drains faster. Real tornadoes are also vortexes, though they form from rotating storm winds.

kids.try: Flip the bottles, swirl, and watch the twister form!
kids.why: Twister! When you swirl, the water spins around and leaves a tunnel in the middle, just like a tornado's funnel!

experiments.realworld: Whirlpools, bathtub drains and hurricanes are all vortexes.

needs: A tornado tube connector or strong duct tape
steps: Fill one bottle about two-thirds with water.
Connect the empty bottle on top with the connector or tape it tightly.
Flip so the water is on top and swirl in circles. Don't shake!

sources.title: NOAA: Tornado in a Bottle
NC State Extension: Tornado in a Bottle

experiments.predict: Will the swirled water drain faster or slower than water you just flip?
experiments.reveal: A funnel forms and the swirled water drains noticeably faster.

experiments.title: The Greenhouse in a Jar
experiments.hook: Cover a thermometer with a glass jar in the sun, and it climbs higher than one left open.

grown.try: Set two thermometers in the sun, one under a glass jar, and compare them every 5 minutes.
grown.why: Sunlight passes through the glass and warms the inside. The warm air is trapped, and heat can't escape as easily, so the covered thermometer rises faster and higher. It's a model of the greenhouse effect: gases in Earth's atmosphere trap heat in a similar (though not identical) way, keeping the planet warmer than it would be otherwise.

kids.try: Two thermometers in the sun. Cover one with a jar. Which gets hotter?
kids.why: Toasty! The jar lets sunlight in but traps the heat, so it gets warmer inside. Earth's air works a little like that jar!

experiments.realworld: Cars parked in the sun get dangerously hot for the same reason, which is why you never leave pets or kids inside.

steps: Place both thermometers side by side in the sun and write down the starting temperatures.
Cover one with the upside-down jar.
Check both every 5 minutes for half an hour.

sources.title: Scientific American / Science Buddies: Heating with the Greenhouse Effect
NASA Climate Kids: What Is the Greenhouse Effect?
Science World: Exploring the Greenhouse Effect

experiments.predict: Which thermometer will be warmer after 30 minutes?
experiments.reveal: The thermometer under the jar climbs faster and ends up warmer.

experiments.title: Can Plants Stop a Landslide?
experiments.hook: Roots act like a net. Pour 'rain' on bare soil and on planted soil, and the difference is shocking.

grown.try: Tilt two pans of soil, one bare and one with grass or sprouts, and pour the same amount of water on each.
grown.why: Runoff is rainwater that flows over the surface when soil can't absorb it, and it carries soil away. Plant roots hold soil together and help absorb water, so the planted pan loses far less soil. That's why bare farm fields and hillsides after wildfires are at higher risk of erosion.

kids.try: Bare dirt vs. dirt with plants. Make it rain. Which washes away?
kids.why: Muddy! The bare dirt washes right off. But plant roots grab the soil and hold on tight like a net!

experiments.realworld: Farmers plant cover crops and cities plant hillsides to keep soil from washing away.

needs: Grass seed or sprouts (grow 1-2 weeks first)
steps: Fill both pans with soil; plant one with grass seed and let it grow.
Prop both pans at the same angle with cups below the low ends.
Pour the same amount of water on each and compare the muddy runoff.

sources.title: Science Buddies: Explore Soil Erosion and See What a Plant Can Do
Scientific American: Can Plants Help Slow Soil Erosion?
USDA Agricultural Research Service: Soil Erosion Lab

experiments.predict: Which pan will lose more soil?
experiments.reveal: The bare pan's runoff is much muddier. The roots hold the planted soil in place.

experiments.title: The Water Cycle in a Bag
experiments.hook: The water you drink today has been rain, clouds and ocean countless times. You can watch the loop in a sandwich bag.

grown.try: Put a little water in a zip bag, seal it, and tape it to a sunny window. Check it through the day.
grown.why: Sunlight warms the water, which evaporates into vapor. When the vapor touches the cooler plastic, it condenses into droplets, like clouds. The drops grow, roll down (precipitation) and collect at the bottom again. It's a sealed model of the planet's water cycle, powered by the Sun.

kids.try: Water in a bag, bag on a sunny window. Watch it 'rain'!
kids.why: Your own mini weather! The sun turns the water into invisible vapor, it turns back into drops on the bag, and then it 'rains' down. Round and round!

experiments.realworld: The U.S. Geological Survey estimates Earth's total water supply at about 326 million cubic miles, and it keeps cycling.

steps: Pour a little water into the bag and seal it tightly.
Tape the bag to a sunny window.
Check it morning, noon and evening. Look for droplets and 'rain'.

sources.title: Science Buddies: Water Cycle in a Bag
Science Museum Oklahoma: Water Cycle in a Bag

experiments.predict: Where will water droplets show up first?
experiments.reveal: Droplets form on the upper sides of the bag and trickle back down as 'rain'.

experiments.title: Buildings That Ride Out Earthquakes
experiments.hook: Some buildings survive earthquakes by sitting on bearings that let the ground move underneath them.

grown.try: Build a block tower on a tray and shake it. Then put the tower on a second tray resting on marbles and shake again.
grown.why: Base isolation separates a building from the ground. When the ground shakes, inertia keeps the building mostly in place while the bearings, here marbles, let the base slide. Engineers test real designs on shake tables. Base isolation is especially useful for shorter, stiffer buildings.

kids.try: Shake a tower. Then put it on marbles and shake again. Which one stands?
kids.why: Wobble, wobble! On the marbles, the ground moves but the tower mostly stays still. Real buildings use giant rubber pads to do this!

experiments.realworld: Hospitals and other critical buildings in earthquake zones often use base isolation bearings.

steps: Build a tall block tower on the small tray and shake the tray side to side.
Rebuild it, then set the small tray on top of marbles inside the big tray.
Shake the big tray the same way and compare.

sources.title: Scientific American / Science Buddies: Earthquake Rollers
Carleton College SERC (Purdue University): Base Isolation for Earthquake Resistance

experiments.predict: Will the tower on marbles shake more or less?
experiments.reveal: The tower on marbles moves much less and usually stays standing.

experiments.title: Jump on Every Planet
experiments.hook: A jump that lifts you 1 foot on Earth would lift you about 14 feet on Pluto.

grown.try: Enter how high you can jump on Earth and see how high you'd go on every world.
grown.why: Your legs push off with the same speed everywhere, but weaker gravity slows you down less, so you rise higher and hang in the air longer. Jump height scales with one divided by the surface gravity. NASA's fact sheet lists gravity relative to Earth: Moon 0.166, Mars 0.377, Jupiter 2.36, Pluto 0.071. (Gas giants have no solid surface; their value is measured at the cloud level where pressure equals Earth's.)

kids.try: Type how high you can jump. Then hop across the solar system!
kids.why: Boing! On the Moon you'd jump about 6 times higher than on Earth. On Jupiter, you could barely get off the ground!

experiments.realworld: Apollo astronauts bounded across the Moon because its gravity is about one-sixth of Earth's.

steps: Stand next to a wall and reach up; mark the spot.
Jump and touch the wall as high as you can; mark it.
Measure between the marks. That's your Earth jump. Enter it above!

sources.title: NASA Planetary Fact Sheet: Values compared to Earth
NASA Planetary Fact Sheet Notes (gravity definition)

experiments.title: Why the Moon Changes Shape
experiments.hook: The Moon is always half lit by the Sun. What changes is how much of the lit half we can see.

grown.try: In a dark room, hold a ball at arm's length near a lamp and turn slowly in a circle. Watch the lit part change.
grown.why: The lamp is the Sun, the ball is the Moon and your head is Earth. As the Moon orbits, we see different amounts of its sunlit half: new moon, crescent, quarter, gibbous, full and back. It isn't Earth's shadow, a common misconception. Earth's shadow causes lunar eclipses instead, which you can model by blocking the lamp with your head.

kids.try: Lamp = Sun. Ball = Moon. You = Earth. Spin slowly and watch!
kids.why: Moon magic solved! The Sun always lights half the Moon. As the Moon goes around us, we see more or less of the bright side!

experiments.realworld: Every month, the Moon goes through all its phases in about 29.5 days.

needs: A ball (or foam ball on a pencil)
steps: Turn on the lamp and stand a few steps away, facing it.
Hold the ball at arm's length, slightly above your head.
Turn slowly to your left in a full circle and watch the lit part grow and shrink.

sources.title: NASA JPL Education: Moon Phases
NASA Science: Lunar Activities

experiments.predict: When the ball is directly opposite the lamp, what phase will you see?
experiments.reveal: Opposite the lamp, the ball looks fully lit: a full moon.

experiments.title: Make Your Own Moon Craters
experiments.hook: The Moon's craters were blasted out by space rocks. Drop marbles into flour and you'll see the same splash patterns.

grown.try: Fill a pan with flour, dust cocoa on top, and drop marbles from different heights.
grown.why: When an impactor hits, it pushes material outward, digging a crater and throwing out bright 'rays' of ejecta, which the cocoa layer reveals. Faster impacts (from higher drops) and bigger impactors make bigger craters. The Moon keeps its craters for billions of years because it has no air, water or weather to erase them.

kids.try: Flour + cocoa + marbles. Drop from low, then high!
kids.why: Splat! Every marble blasts out a crater with streaks around it, just like the real ones on the Moon!

experiments.realworld: Earth gets hit too, but wind, water and plants slowly erase most craters. The Moon keeps them all.

steps: Fill the pan with about an inch of flour and smooth it.
Sift a thin layer of cocoa on top.
Drop marbles from different heights and measure the craters.

sources.title: NASA JPL Education: Make a Moon Crater
The Planetary Society: Crater Simulator

experiments.predict: Will a marble dropped from higher make a bigger or smaller crater?
experiments.reveal: Higher drops make wider craters with longer streaks of flour.

experiments.title: How Far Away Are the Planets, Really?
experiments.hook: If you fold a strip of paper in half, Uranus lands right at the middle and the inner planets crowd into one tiny end.

grown.try: Use a long strip of paper as the solar system, guess where each planet goes, then fold to find the real spots.
grown.why: Most pictures squeeze the planets together. NASA JPL's Solar System Scroll uses folding (halves, quarters, eighths) to place planets at their true relative distances. Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars all land within the first small fraction of the strip, while the outer planets spread far apart.

kids.try: Guess where each planet goes on the strip. Then fold to check!
kids.why: Whoa, space is HUGE! The four rocky planets all squish near the Sun, and the rest are super far apart!

experiments.realworld: Spacecraft take years to reach the outer planets because the distances are so enormous.

needs: A long strip of paper (receipt tape or toilet paper)
steps: Mark the Sun at one end and Neptune at the other, then mark your guesses.
Fold the strip in half: the middle is Uranus.
Keep folding into quarters and eighths following NASA JPL's guide to place the rest.

sources.title: NASA JPL Education: Solar System Scroll
NASA JPL Education: Make a Scale Solar System
Exploratorium: Build a Solar System

experiments.predict: Where do you think Earth will land on the strip?
experiments.reveal: Earth ends up very close to the Sun end, far closer than most people guess.

experiments.title: The Balloon Rocket
experiments.hook: Rockets don't push against the ground or air. They push stuff out the back, and that push sends them forward.

grown.try: Tape an inflated (untied) balloon to a straw on a string stretched across the room, then let go.
grown.why: Newton's third law: for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. Air rushes out the back of the balloon (action), and the balloon is pushed forward (reaction). Real rockets do the same with hot exhaust gases, which is why they work even in the vacuum of space.

kids.try: String through a straw, balloon on the straw, let go!
kids.why: Zoom! The air shoots out the back and pushes the balloon forward. Real rockets work the exact same way!

experiments.realworld: NASA's rockets follow the same law, using exhaust gases instead of air.

steps: Thread the string through the straw and tie it tight between two chairs.
Blow up the balloon and pinch it closed. Don't tie it.
Tape it to the straw, pull it to one end, and let go.

sources.title: NASA JPL Education: Simple Rocket Science
NASA Glenn: Newton's Third Law and Rocket Propulsion
Science Friday: Balloon Rockets

experiments.predict: Which way will the balloon go when you let go?
experiments.reveal: The balloon zips along the string in the direction opposite the escaping air.

experiments.title: Why We Only See One Side of the Moon
experiments.hook: The Moon does spin, exactly once each time it circles Earth. That's why the same face always points at us.

grown.try: Walk in a circle around a chair while always facing it. Notice you also turned all the way around the room.
grown.why: The Moon is tidally locked: Earth's gravity long ago slowed its spin until one rotation matched one orbit. So the same side, the near side, always faces us. No one saw the far side until the Soviet Luna 3 spacecraft photographed it in 1959. Small wobbles called libration let us see a bit more than half over time.

kids.try: Circle a chair while staring at it. Did you spin too?
kids.why: Sneaky Moon! It spins exactly as fast as it goes around us, so it always shows us the same face, like you staring at the chair!

experiments.realworld: Many moons in the solar system are tidally locked to their planets.

steps: Put a chair in the middle of the room. You are the Moon; the chair is Earth.
Walk a full circle around the chair while always facing it.
Notice that your body also turned to face every wall: one spin per orbit.

sources.title: University of Hawaii: Tidal Locking, Why the Man in the Moon Can Always See You
Live Science: Why can't we see the far side of the moon?

experiments.predict: While circling the chair and facing it, do you rotate at all?
experiments.reveal: Yes, exactly once per lap. That's synchronous rotation, just like the Moon.

experiments.title: Hold Strawberry DNA in Your Hand
experiments.hook: You can pull real DNA out of a strawberry with dish soap, salt and rubbing alcohol, and see it with your own eyes.

grown.try: Mash strawberries with soapy salt water, filter it, and gently pour cold rubbing alcohol on top.
grown.why: Detergent breaks open cell and nuclear membranes, releasing DNA. Salt helps the DNA strands clump together. DNA doesn't dissolve in alcohol, so it comes out of solution as white, stringy goo at the layer between liquids. Strawberries work especially well because they are octoploid: they carry eight copies of each chromosome.

kids.try: Smash, mix, filter, add alcohol. Watch white strands appear!
kids.why: Wow! That white goo is real DNA, the instructions that built the strawberry! Strawberries have tons of it, so you can actually see it!

experiments.realworld: Scientists extract DNA the same basic way for genetic testing and research.

steps: Smash the strawberries in the bag for 2 minutes.
Mix soap, salt and water, add 2 spoonfuls to the bag, and mash 1 more minute. Filter into a cup.
Slowly pour cold rubbing alcohol down the side. Wait a minute, then lift the white strands with a toothpick.
home.safety: Grown-up needed. Rubbing alcohol is poisonous and flammable. Don't eat anything from this experiment.

sources.title: National Human Genome Research Institute: How to extract DNA from a strawberry
Utah Agriculture in the Classroom: Strawberry DNA Extraction Lab

experiments.predict: What do you think DNA will look like?
experiments.reveal: Cloudy white strands collect between the layers and can be lifted out.

experiments.title: Watch a Plant Drink
experiments.hook: Plants pull water up through tiny tubes, and you can see them when you add food coloring.

grown.try: Stand a celery stalk with leaves in colored water overnight, then cut it crosswise.
grown.why: Water travels up through tubes called xylem, driven mostly by transpiration, water evaporating from the leaves and pulling more water up behind it, plus capillary action. The dye rides along, coloring the leaves and showing the xylem as colored dots in the cut stalk.

kids.try: Celery in colored water. Wait. Then cut it and look!
kids.why: Slurp! The celery drinks the colored water through tiny straws inside, all the way up to its leaves!

experiments.realworld: Tall trees lift water more than 100 feet using this same pulling effect.

steps: Add lots of food coloring to the water.
Stand the celery in it overnight.
Have a grown-up cut the stalk across and look for colored dots.

sources.title: Science Buddies: Plant Water Transport lesson
Science World: Capillary Action
John Innes Centre: Visualise xylem

experiments.predict: Where will the color show up by tomorrow?
experiments.reveal: The leaves tint with the color and the cut stalk shows colored dots: the xylem.

experiments.title: The Living Balloon Inflater
experiments.hook: Those dry grains of baker's yeast are alive. Feed them sugar and they'll inflate a balloon for you.

grown.try: Mix yeast, sugar and warm water in a bottle and stretch a balloon over the top. Check it every 10 minutes.
grown.why: Yeast are single-celled fungi. When they eat sugar they release carbon dioxide gas, a process called fermentation. With nowhere else to go, the gas fills the balloon. Try one bottle without sugar, or with cold water, to see the yeast slow down.

kids.try: Yeast + sugar + warm water, balloon on top. Wait and watch!
kids.why: It's alive! The yeast gobbles the sugar and burps out gas, and the gas blows up the balloon!

experiments.realworld: Bread rises because yeast fills the dough with carbon dioxide bubbles.

steps: Pour the warm water into the bottle and add the sugar and yeast.
Swirl gently and stretch the balloon over the top.
Check every 10 minutes for about an hour.

sources.title: Science Buddies: Single-Celled Science: Yeasty Beasties
Institute of Food Technologists: Take-home experiments (yeast balloon)

experiments.predict: What will happen without sugar?
experiments.reveal: With sugar, the balloon slowly inflates. Without sugar, it barely changes.

experiments.title: The Plant That Solves a Maze
experiments.hook: Plants can't walk, but they can find their way through a maze to reach light.

grown.try: Build cardboard walls inside a shoebox, cut a hole at one end, and put a bean sprout at the other. Close it up.
grown.why: Plants grow toward light, a response called phototropism. A plant hormone called auxin builds up on the shaded side of the stem, making those cells grow longer, so the stem bends toward the light. Over several days the sprout weaves around the walls to reach the hole.

kids.try: Bean in a box maze. Close it. Peek in a few days!
kids.why: Clever bean! It can't see, but it bends toward the light and finds its way out of the maze!

experiments.realworld: Houseplants lean toward windows for the same reason; turning the pot keeps them straight.

needs: A sprouted bean in a small cup of soil
steps: Cut a hole in one end of the box and tape in 2 cardboard walls with openings on alternating sides.
Put the watered bean sprout at the far end.
Close the box, set it in a sunny spot, and check every few days.

sources.title: Chicago Botanic Garden: How to Train Your Plant
The Children's Museum of Indianapolis: Plant Maze
Texas Agriculture in the Classroom: Phototropism

experiments.predict: Will the bean find its way to the hole?
experiments.reveal: Over a week or two, the stem bends around the walls and grows toward the light.

experiments.title: The Hidden Colors in Green Leaves
experiments.hook: Fall colors aren't added in autumn. They were hiding in the leaf all summer.

grown.try: Mash leaves in rubbing alcohol, warm the jar in hot water, then dip a coffee filter strip in and wait.
grown.why: Leaves contain several pigments: green chlorophyll, yellow and orange carotenoids, and sometimes red anthocyanins. Paper chromatography separates them because each pigment travels up the paper at a different speed. In fall, trees make less chlorophyll, so the other colors show through.

kids.try: Leaves + rubbing alcohol + paper strip. Watch the hidden colors climb!
kids.why: Secret colors! Under all that green, leaves have yellow and orange hiding inside. In fall, the green fades and the hidden colors show off!

experiments.realworld: Scientists use chromatography to separate and identify chemicals in labs every day.

steps: Tear leaves into tiny pieces in a jar and just cover them with rubbing alcohol.
Mash them and set the jar in hot tap water for 30 minutes.
Dip a filter strip so its tip touches the liquid and wait an hour or more.
home.safety: Grown-up needed. Rubbing alcohol is flammable; keep it away from flames.

sources.title: Northern Illinois University STEAM: Simulating Fall in Your Dining Room
Home Science Tools: Leaf Chromatography

experiments.predict: Will you see only green on the strip?
experiments.reveal: Bands of green and yellow (sometimes orange) separate as they climb the paper.

experiments.title: The Potato That Fizzes
experiments.hook: A slice of raw potato can make hydrogen peroxide bubble, thanks to an enzyme found in almost all living things.

grown.try: Put a slice of raw potato in a dish and pour a little 3% hydrogen peroxide on it.
grown.why: Living cells make hydrogen peroxide as a byproduct, and it's harmful in large amounts. Catalase, an enzyme found in most living things exposed to oxygen, rapidly breaks it into water and oxygen gas, which you see as bubbles. It's the same enzyme that makes peroxide fizz on a cut.

kids.try: Raw potato + a few drops of peroxide. Look closely!
kids.why: Fizz! The potato has a helper called catalase that breaks peroxide into water and oxygen bubbles. You have it too!

experiments.realworld: Cooking destroys enzymes. Try a cooked potato slice and see the difference.

steps: Put the raw potato slice in the dish.
Pour a little hydrogen peroxide on it and watch.
Repeat with a cooked slice and compare.
home.safety: Grown-up needed. Keep peroxide out of eyes; use only 3% store-bought.

sources.title: USDA Agricultural Research Service: Elephant Toothpaste (catalase)
Northern Virginia Community College: Elephant Toothpaste (potato catalase)

experiments.predict: Will the cooked potato fizz as much as the raw one?
experiments.reveal: The raw slice bubbles; the cooked slice barely does, because heat destroys the enzyme.

experiments.title: Find the Highest Sound You Can Hear
experiments.hook: Young ears hear up to about 20,000 vibrations per second. As we age, the highest pitches fade first.

grown.try: Start the tone at a low volume and slide it higher until it disappears. Note the number.
grown.why: Pitch is set by frequency, measured in hertz (vibrations per second). A healthy young person hears roughly 20 to 20,000 Hz, and high-frequency hearing is gradually lost with age and noise exposure. Note: phone and laptop speakers often can't play the very lowest or highest tones, so your result also depends on your device.

kids.try: Turn your volume LOW. Slide the tone higher until you can't hear it!
kids.why: Beep! Kids can usually hear really high squeaky sounds that grown-ups can't. Try it with your family and compare!

experiments.realworld: Audiologists test hearing at many different pitches, because high-pitch loss often comes first.

needs: A family member to compare with
steps: Set your device volume low before starting.
Slide the tone slowly upward until it disappears.
Have family members try and compare numbers.
home.safety: Keep the volume low. Loud high tones can be uncomfortable and loud sound can damage hearing.

sources.title: Simon Fraser University: Range of Human Hearing
The Physics Factbook: Frequency Range of Human Hearing

experiments.title: A Rainbow from a Glass of Water
experiments.hook: Sunlight looks white, but it's every color mixed together, and a glass of water can pull them apart.

grown.try: On a sunny day, set a glass of water on white paper in the sunlight and look for a rainbow.
grown.why: Light slows down when it enters water and bends, which is called refraction. Each color bends a slightly different amount, so white light spreads into a spectrum. Raindrops do the same in the sky. Isaac Newton used a glass prism to prove sunlight is a mix of colors.

kids.try: Sun + glass of water + white paper. Find the rainbow!
kids.why: Rainbow! The water bends the sunlight and splits it into all its colors, just like raindrops do!

experiments.realworld: Every rainbow in the sky is made by millions of raindrops acting like tiny prisms.

needs: Sunshine (or a flashlight in a dark room)
steps: Fill the glass about three-quarters full.
Set it in sunlight near the edge of a table, over white paper.
Move the glass and paper until a rainbow appears.

sources.title: Science Buddies: Make a Rainbow
Lawrence Hall of Science: Make a Prism
Scientific American: Make Your Own Rainbow

experiments.predict: Which color will be on the outside edge of your rainbow?
experiments.reveal: A band of colors appears on the paper, from red on one side to violet on the other.

experiments.title: A Sunset in a Glass
experiments.hook: The sky is blue and sunsets are red for the same reason, and a few drops of milk can show you why.

grown.try: In a dark room, shine a flashlight through a glass of water with a little milk. Look from the side, then from the end.
grown.why: Tiny particles scatter short-wavelength blue light much more than long-wavelength red light, an effect called Rayleigh scattering. From the side the milky water looks bluish, like the sky. Looking through it, the light looks orange, like a sunset, because the blue was scattered away. At sunset, sunlight travels through much more air.

kids.try: Milky water + flashlight. Look from the side, then look through it!
kids.why: Sky in a glass! From the side it looks a little blue like the daytime sky. Look through it and it turns orange like a sunset!

experiments.realworld: Smoke and dust in the air can make sunsets extra red.

steps: Fill the glass with water and stir in a little milk.
Shine the flashlight through the side of the glass.
Look from the side, then look straight through toward the light. Add a little more milk and compare.

sources.title: Science Buddies: Sunset Colors in a Glass
American Physical Society Physics at Home: Big O' Glass of Sunset
WebExhibits Causes of Color: Sunset in a Glass

experiments.predict: What color will the light look when you look straight through the milky water?
experiments.reveal: From the side the water looks faintly blue; looking through it, the light looks orange-yellow.

experiments.title: The Pencil That Breaks in Water
experiments.hook: A straight pencil looks snapped in half the moment you dip it in water.

grown.try: Put a pencil in a glass of water and look from the side as you move it around.
grown.why: Light travels slower in water than in air, so it bends when it crosses the water's surface. Your brain assumes light travels in straight lines, so the underwater part appears shifted, and the round glass magnifies it too, making it look wider.

kids.try: Pencil in water. Look from the side. Is it broken?
kids.why: Optical trick! The light bends when it leaves the water, so the pencil looks broken. Pull it out and it's fine!

experiments.realworld: This is why spearfishers aim below where a fish appears, and why pools look shallower than they are.

steps: Fill the glass about halfway with water.
Place the pencil in at a slant.
Look from the side and slide the pencil around the glass.

sources.title: The Physics Classroom: The Broken Pencil
The Physics Classroom: Refraction and line of sight
Museums Victoria Scienceworks: Experiment with bending light

experiments.predict: Where will the pencil look broken?
experiments.reveal: It appears shifted right at the water surface, and wider underwater.

experiments.title: The Cup-and-String Telephone
experiments.hook: Sound travels better through a tight string than through air.

grown.try: Connect two cups with a long string, pull it tight, and talk into one cup while a friend listens.
grown.why: Your voice vibrates the air in the cup, which vibrates the cup's bottom. A tight string carries those vibrations to the other cup, which turns them back into sound. If the string sags or someone pinches it, the vibrations stop and the sound fades.

kids.try: Two cups, one tight string. Whisper a secret!
kids.why: Hello?! Your voice shakes the cup, the shake zips down the string, and the other cup turns it back into sound!

experiments.realworld: Doctors' stethoscopes also carry sound vibrations straight to your ears.

steps: Poke a small hole in the bottom of each cup.
Thread the string through and knot it inside each cup.
Walk apart until the string is tight. One talks, one listens. Then let the string sag.

sources.title: Scientific American: Talk through a String Telephone
TeachEngineering: String Telephones

experiments.predict: What happens if the string goes slack?
experiments.reveal: Tight: you hear clearly. Slack or pinched: the sound mostly disappears.

experiments.title: Play Music on Water Glasses
experiments.hook: Tap a glass and it rings. Add water and the note goes down.

grown.try: Line up identical glasses with different amounts of water and tap each one gently with a spoon.
grown.why: Tapping makes the glass vibrate, and the vibrating glass shakes the air. Water adds mass that the glass has to move, so it vibrates more slowly, producing a lower pitch. The glass with the most water plays the lowest note.

kids.try: Glasses with different water levels. Tap and listen!
kids.why: Ding! More water makes the glass wiggle slower, so the note gets lower. Make a scale and play a song!

experiments.realworld: Musical instruments work on the same idea: bigger or heavier parts vibrate slower and play lower notes.

steps: Fill the glasses with steadily less water, from nearly full to almost empty.
Tap each glass gently near the top.
Add or pour out water to tune them into a scale.

sources.title: Home Science Tools: Simple Water Glass Xylophone
Libraries NI: Design your own Water Xylophone

experiments.predict: Which glass will play the lowest note?
experiments.reveal: The fullest glass plays the lowest note; the emptiest plays the highest.

experiments.title: Count Like a Computer
experiments.hook: With just five cards, a computer's way of counting can show every number from 0 to 31.

grown.try: Flip the cards to make numbers. Each card is on (1) or off (0). Try to make your age.
grown.why: Computers store everything as bits, 1s and 0s. Each place in binary is worth double the one before: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Add the cards that are face up to get the number. Five bits can show 0 to 31; eight bits, called a byte, can show 0 to 255. This is Computer Science Unplugged's classic Count the Dots activity.

kids.try: Flip the cards to make numbers! Can you make 7? 19? Your age?
kids.why: Beep boop! Computers count with only 1s and 0s. Each card is worth double the last one. Flip them to make any number up to 31!

experiments.realworld: Every photo, song and message on your phone is stored as billions of 1s and 0s.

steps: Draw 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 dots on the cards.
Lay them in a row: 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.
Flip cards face up or down to make numbers. Count to 31 on one hand with fingers up (1) or down (0).

sources.title: CS Unplugged: How Binary Digits Work
Harvey Mudd College / CS Unplugged: Binary Numbers worksheet

experiments.title: Power a Light with Lemons
experiments.hook: A lemon, a copper wire and a zinc-coated nail make a real battery.

grown.try: Push a copper strip and a galvanized nail into each lemon, link several lemons copper-to-zinc, and connect a small LED.
grown.why: Two different metals in an acid make a simple battery. Zinc reacts with the lemon's citric acid and gives up electrons, which flow through the wire toward the copper. One lemon usually isn't enough to light an LED, so you connect several in series, copper to zinc, to add up the voltage. Commercial batteries use the same principle.

kids.try: Copper + zinc + lemon. Link a few together and light the LED!
kids.why: Zap! The lemon juice and two different metals push tiny electrons through the wire. Hook up a few lemons and your light turns on!

experiments.realworld: Every battery in your house is two different materials and a chemical between them.

needs: 4 copper strips or heavy copper wire
A small LED (2 volts or less)
steps: Roll the lemons to loosen the juice, then push a nail and a copper strip into each, apart.
Connect copper of lemon 1 to the nail of lemon 2, and so on.
Attach the LED's long leg to the free copper and short leg to the free nail.
home.safety: Don't eat the lemons afterward.

sources.title: Science World: Lemon Battery
Australian National University: How to make a lemon battery

experiments.predict: Will one lemon light the LED, or will you need more?
experiments.reveal: One lemon usually isn't enough; several in a row together can make the LED glow dimly.

experiments.title: Turn a Nail into a Magnet
experiments.hook: Electricity and magnetism are two sides of the same force. Wrap a wire around a nail and you can switch a magnet on and off.

grown.try: Wrap insulated wire around an iron nail many times, connect the ends to a battery, and pick up paper clips.
grown.why: Electric current flowing through a wire creates a magnetic field. Coiling the wire concentrates that field, and the iron nail strengthens it further. More turns of wire make a stronger magnet. Disconnect the battery and the magnetism mostly disappears. Jefferson Lab uses huge electromagnets to steer its particle beams.

kids.try: Wire around a nail, ends on a battery. Pick up paper clips!
kids.why: Magnet on, magnet off! Electricity running around the nail turns it into a magnet. Unhook the battery, and the clips drop!

experiments.realworld: Electromagnets are in speakers, motors, doorbells, MRI machines and scrapyard cranes.

steps: Leave 8 inches of wire free, then wrap the rest tightly around the nail in one direction.
A grown-up strips the insulation off both ends.
Tape the ends to the battery terminals and touch the nail to paper clips. Disconnect to drop them.
home.safety: Grown-up needed. The wire and battery can get hot; disconnect between tests. Don't use rechargeable batteries.

sources.title: Jefferson Lab: How do you make an electromagnet?
National MagLab: Making Electromagnets

experiments.predict: What will happen if you add more turns of wire?
experiments.reveal: The nail picks up paper clips, and more turns pick up more.

experiments.title: Measure the Speed of Light with Chocolate
experiments.hook: Your microwave and a chocolate bar can measure the fastest speed in the universe.

grown.try: Remove the turntable, microwave a chocolate bar briefly, measure the distance between melted spots, and do one multiplication.
grown.why: A microwave oven makes a standing wave with hot spots. Melted spots are about half a wavelength apart. Most ovens run at 2.45 billion cycles per second (check the label). Speed = wavelength x frequency. Spots 6 cm apart mean a 12 cm wavelength: 0.12 m x 2,450,000,000 = about 294,000,000 m/s, close to the defined speed of light, 299,792,458 m/s.

kids.try: Chocolate in the microwave, no spinning. Measure the melted spots and multiply!
kids.why: Light-speed snack! The microwave melts the chocolate in a pattern. Measure the gaps, do some math, and you get the speed of light!

experiments.realworld: Microwaves, radio, Wi-Fi and visible light are all the same kind of wave traveling at the same speed.

steps: Take out the turntable so the plate won't spin. Put the chocolate on the plate.
Heat about 20-30 seconds, just until a few spots soften.
Measure between two melted spots in centimeters, double it, convert to meters and multiply by 2,450,000,000.
home.safety: Grown-up needed. Chocolate and plates get hot; never run an empty microwave.

sources.title: Jefferson Lab: Measure the Speed of Light, With Chocolate!
The Open University: Measure the speed of light with your microwave

experiments.predict: How far apart do you think the melted spots will be?
experiments.reveal: Melted spots usually appear about 6 cm apart, giving a speed close to 300,000,000 m/s.

experiments.title: Make a Compass from a Needle
experiments.hook: Earth is a giant magnet. A magnetized needle floating on water will swing to line up with it.

grown.try: Stroke a needle with a magnet, push it through a slice of cork, and float it in a bowl of water.
grown.why: Stroking the needle in one direction lines up tiny magnetic regions in the steel, turning it into a weak magnet. Floating it lets it turn freely, so it aligns with Earth's magnetic field and points roughly north-south. Sailors relied on magnetic compasses for centuries.

kids.try: Magnet the needle, float it on cork, and see where it points!
kids.why: Point north! The needle becomes a tiny magnet, and Earth's giant magnet spins it to point north and south!

experiments.realworld: Phones still have a tiny magnetometer, an electronic compass, inside.

steps: Stroke the needle with one end of the magnet about 20 times, in one direction only.
Use pliers to push the needle through the cork slice.
Float it in the middle of the bowl, away from the magnet, and watch it settle.
home.safety: Grown-up needed. Needles are sharp; use pliers.

sources.title: Science Buddies: Make a Magnetic Compass
National Park Service: How to Make Your Own Compass

experiments.predict: Which direction will the needle settle?
experiments.reveal: It turns and settles pointing roughly north-south.

experiments.title: Make a Stylus for Your Phone
experiments.hook: Touchscreens don't feel pressure. They sense the electricity in your body.

grown.try: Wrap foil around a pen so it touches a damp cotton swab tip, hold the foil, and tap your screen.
grown.why: Most phones and tablets have capacitive touchscreens that monitor an electric field across the screen. Your body conducts electricity, so a fingertip changes the field where you touch. A plain plastic pen does nothing, but foil connects your hand to the tip, so the screen senses the stylus like a finger.

kids.try: Foil pen + damp swab. Hold the foil and tap the screen!
kids.why: Tap tap! Your body is a little bit electric. The foil carries that to the tip, so the phone thinks it's your finger!

experiments.realworld: That's why ordinary gloves don't work on touchscreens, but special conductive gloves do.

steps: Cut the swab short and push it into the pen's tip so cotton sticks out.
Wrap foil around the pen so it touches the cotton, and tape it.
Dampen the tip slightly, hold the foil, and tap the screen. Then try without touching the foil.
home.safety: Use only a little water; never get your device wet.

sources.title: Make: DIY Capacitive Stylus
DIY.org: Learn to Make a Pen Stylus

experiments.predict: Will the stylus work if you hold it by the plastic instead of the foil?
experiments.reveal: It works when your hand touches the foil, and usually stops when it doesn't.

experiments.title: The Paper Bridge Challenge
experiments.hook: A flat sheet of paper collapses under one coin. Fold it like an accordion and it holds a stack.

grown.try: Lay paper across two cups and add pennies until it fails. Then fold the same paper accordion-style and test again.
grown.why: Strength depends on shape as well as material. Folds make the paper deeper and stiffer, so it resists bending. Engineers use the same idea in corrugated cardboard, metal roofing, truss bridges and I-beams.

kids.try: Flat paper bridge vs. folded paper bridge. Load it with pennies!
kids.why: Super paper! A flat sheet flops, but fold it into zigzags and it can hold a pile of pennies. Same paper, smarter shape!

experiments.realworld: Corrugated cardboard boxes are strong for exactly this reason.

steps: Lay a flat sheet across the gap and add pennies one at a time. Count before it falls.
Fold a new sheet accordion-style the long way.
Test it the same way. Then invent your own fold.

sources.title: PBS KIDS for Parents: Build and Test Paper Bridges
Explore Engineering / Engineers Nova Scotia: Strengthen a Paper Bridge

experiments.predict: How many more pennies will the folded bridge hold?
experiments.reveal: The folded bridge usually holds many times more pennies than the flat sheet.

experiments.title: The Spaghetti Tower
experiments.hook: Twenty sticks of dry spaghetti, tape, string and one marshmallow. How tall can you go?

grown.try: In 18 minutes, build the tallest freestanding tower that holds a marshmallow on top.
grown.why: Spaghetti is strong when pulled (tension) but snaps easily when squeezed or bent (compression). Triangles and wide bases make structures stable. The challenge is famous in engineering classes because it rewards testing early and redesigning.

kids.try: Build the tallest tower that holds a marshmallow. Go!
kids.why: Engineer time! Triangles and a wide bottom are your secret weapons. Test early, fix it, and build higher!

experiments.realworld: Real towers and bridges use triangles, called trusses, because they don't bend out of shape.

steps: Set a timer for 18 minutes.
Build a freestanding tower; spaghetti, tape and string can be broken or cut.
Put the marshmallow on top and measure when time is up.

sources.title: TeachEngineering: Leaning Tower of Pasta
NASA JPL Education: Spaghetti, Anyone?

experiments.predict: Will a wide base or a narrow base let you build taller?
experiments.reveal: Towers with wide, triangle-braced bases usually stand tallest.

experiments.title: The Straw Rocket
experiments.hook: A rocket made from paper and a drinking straw can fly across the room on one breath.

grown.try: Roll paper around a pencil, tape a nose cone and fins, slide it onto a straw, and blow.
grown.why: Your breath pushes air into the closed paper tube, launching the rocket. Fins keep it stable so it flies straight. NASA JPL challenges students to change one thing at a time (length, fin shape or angle) and measure the result, which is the engineering design process.

kids.try: Build it, launch it, measure it. Then change one thing and launch again!
kids.why: Blast off! Your breath is the rocket fuel. Fins keep it flying straight. Change the design to make it fly farther!

experiments.realworld: NASA engineers test rocket designs the same way: change one variable and measure.

steps: Roll a paper strip around a pencil and tape it. Pinch and tape one end closed as a nose.
Add paper fins at the other end. Remove the pencil.
Slide the rocket onto the straw, aim at a clear area, blow, and measure.
home.safety: Never aim at people or faces.

sources.title: NASA JPL Education: Make a Straw Rocket
NASA JPL Education: Straw Rockets (lesson)
Science Buddies: Build a Paper Rocket

experiments.predict: Will a longer or shorter rocket fly farther?
experiments.reveal: Results vary by design, so testing one change at a time shows what works best.

experiments.title: The Foil Boat Challenge
experiments.hook: A ball of foil sinks. The same foil shaped into a boat can carry dozens of pennies.

grown.try: Shape a square of foil into a boat and add pennies one at a time until it sinks. Then redesign.
grown.why: A boat floats when the water it pushes aside weighs as much as the boat and its load. Spreading the foil into a wide hull displaces more water, so it supports more weight. Spreading the pennies evenly keeps it stable, and steel ships float for the same reason.

kids.try: Build a foil boat. How many pennies before it sinks?
kids.why: Ahoy! A crumpled ball sinks, but a wide boat shape pushes away lots of water and floats with tons of pennies!

experiments.realworld: Giant steel cargo ships float because their hulls push aside an enormous amount of water.

steps: Shape one foil square into a boat.
Float it and add pennies one at a time, spreading them out.
Count, then try a new shape with a fresh square.

sources.title: Science Buddies: How Much Weight Can Your Boat Float?
NOAA: Build a Boat

experiments.predict: Which hull shape will hold the most: tall and narrow or wide and flat?
experiments.reveal: Wide, flat-bottomed boats with low walls usually hold the most pennies.

experiments.title: The Egg Drop Lander
experiments.hook: NASA landed rovers on Mars using giant airbags. Can you land an egg without breaking it?

grown.try: Design a package that protects a raw egg dropped from a set height, then test and improve it.
grown.why: A falling egg gains speed and energy. To survive, a lander must slow down (like a parachute), absorb the impact over more time (cushioning or airbags), and protect the egg on all sides. NASA used airbag landing systems for several Mars missions.

kids.try: Build a lander. Drop your egg. Did it survive? Redesign and go higher!
kids.why: Egg-stronaut mission! Slow it down, cushion the crash and protect every side. NASA did this for real with Mars rovers!

experiments.realworld: Car crumple zones and bike helmets work by spreading out the force of an impact.

needs: Straws, paper, tape, cups, balloons, cotton or plastic bags
steps: Pick a drop height (start with about 5 feet).
Build a lander around the egg using your materials.
Drop it, check the egg, redesign, and try a higher drop.
home.safety: Drop only from safe heights, never from windows or roofs. Grown-up should choose the spot.

sources.title: NASA: Egg Drop Lander
PBS KIDS Design Squad: Soft Landing
Science World: Egg Drop

experiments.predict: Will a parachute, cushioning, or both protect the egg best?
experiments.reveal: Designs that both slow the fall and cushion the egg usually survive the highest drops.

experiments.title: The Balloon-Powered Car
experiments.hook: Escaping air can drive a car across the floor using the same law that launches rockets.

grown.try: Build a car from a bottle or cardboard with straw axles and bottle-cap wheels, and power it with a balloon.
grown.why: Newton's third law: air pushed out the back pushes the car forward. A lighter car accelerates more with the same push (the second law), and friction eventually slows it to a stop (the first law). Science Buddies uses it as an engineering challenge: test, measure and improve.

kids.try: Build it, blow up the balloon, let it zoom. How far did it go?
kids.why: Vroom! Air rushes out the back and pushes the car forward. Make it lighter and it goes even farther!

experiments.realworld: Jet engines push air backward to move planes forward.

steps: Tape two straws across the body and slide skewers through them as axles; attach caps as wheels.
Attach a balloon to a straw with a rubber band; tape the straw on top pointing backward.
Blow up the balloon through the straw, pinch it, set the car down and let go. Measure the distance.

sources.title: Science Buddies: Balloon Car
Science World: Rocket Cars

experiments.predict: Will a lighter car go farther?
experiments.reveal: Lighter, straighter cars with free-spinning wheels usually travel farthest.
